title: Redis: clustering, slots & hot keys
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: Hash slots, MOVED redirects, hash tags and why Redis clusters have no query router, plus the hot key problem and its remedies.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

questions.prompt: How does a Redis cluster decide which node stores a key?

options.text: The key hashes to one of 16,384 slots, and each slot is assigned to a node.
options.why: Right: slot ownership defines placement.

options.text: A central router looks the key up in a global directory.
options.why: There is no central router.

options.text: Nodes take turns, storing each new key in round-robin order.
options.why: Placement is deterministic from the key.

options.text: The client picks any node and the cluster balances it later.
options.why: Clients compute the slot and aim for the right node.

questions.explanation: Choosing keys is how you scale Redis, because the key decides the slot and therefore the node.

questions.prompt: A client asks the wrong node for a key. What happens?

options.text: The node replies MOVED, and the client updates its slot map and retries.
options.why: Right: clients cache the map; nodes do not forward requests.

options.text: The node forwards the request to the right node transparently.
options.why: Redis nodes do not proxy requests.

options.text: The cluster returns an empty value for the key.
options.why: You get a redirect, not a silent miss.

options.text: The cluster restarts so slots are reassigned.
options.why: Nothing restarts; the client just updates its map.

questions.explanation: Clients cache the slot-to-node map so they can hit the correct node on the first try.

questions.prompt: You issue a multi-key command whose keys live on different nodes. What does Redis do?

options.text: It returns an error, because there is no router that splits and merges across nodes.
options.why: Right: all the data for a command must live on one node.

options.text: It splits the command, runs the pieces and merges the results without any extra configuration.
options.why: There is no such query router.

options.text: It runs slowly but correctly by scatter-gather in a typical production setup.
options.why: It fails fast instead of running slowly.

options.text: It silently drops the keys on other nodes.
options.why: You get an explicit error.

questions.explanation: Structure keys so related data shares a slot. Redis fails rather than running a slow cross-node query.

questions.prompt: How do you make {user:123}:posts and {user:123}:likes land on the same node?

options.text: Hash tags: only the part inside braces is hashed, so both keys share a slot.
options.why: Right: ready for a MULTI transaction across both.

options.text: Give both keys the same TTL so they are co-located for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: TTL has no effect on placement.

options.text: Store them in one list under a third key as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: That changes the data model, not the placement rule.

options.text: Run both on a single-node setup only.
options.why: Hash tags work inside a cluster.

questions.explanation: Use hash tags deliberately: they enable multi-key operations but can concentrate load on one slot.

questions.prompt: One product suddenly receives as much traffic as every other product combined. What is this called?

options.text: A hot key: one key absorbing a disproportionate share of traffic, overloading its node.
options.why: Right: even spreading cannot help a single key.

options.text: A cache stampede on the whole cluster in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: A stampede is many requests on an expired key, a different issue.

options.text: A split brain between replicas in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Split brain is a partition problem, not a traffic one.

options.text: A hash slot migration.
options.why: Migration moves slots; it is not a traffic surge.

questions.explanation: Recognise hot keys proactively. Then design remediations and show the trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Select all valid remediations for a read-hot key.

options.text: Keep a small in-memory cache of the hottest items in each app server.
options.why: Yes: most reads never reach Redis, at the cost of staleness.

options.text: Store copies under several keys such as product:123:1 to :10 and read a random one.
options.why: Yes: copies spread across slots and nodes.

options.text: Add read replicas and configure clients to read from them.
options.why: Yes: it multiplies read capacity for that slot.

options.text: Add more primary nodes, since the key will rebalance across them.
options.why: No: one key lives on one slot, however many nodes exist.

questions.explanation: Every fix has a cost: staleness, write fan-out to copies, or replica lag.

questions.prompt: Why do read replicas not fix a write-hot key?

options.text: Every write still lands on the one primary that owns the slot.
options.why: Right: replicas only absorb reads.

options.text: Replicas refuse writes to hot keys by design as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: They simply cannot accept writes.

options.text: Replicas copy only keys that are not hot.
options.why: Replication copies everything.

options.text: Replication cannot be enabled in cluster mode under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Clusters commonly run replicas.

questions.explanation: For write-hot keys, shard the key (for example per-shard counters) and combine reads.

questions.prompt: True or false: cluster clients read from replicas by default, so replicas automatically absorb read load.

options.text: True
options.why: They do not by default.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: you must configure replica reads.

questions.explanation: Clients read from the primary unless configured for replica reads (READONLY), which interviewers like to probe.
